title: AI Didn’t Kill the Web, It Moved in! — Olivier Leplus (AWS) & Yohan Lasorsa (Microsoft)

summary: Yohan Lasorsa (Microsoft, Angular GDE) and Olivier Leplus (AWS, Web GDE) present on how AI has become integral to every stage of web development in 2026. The talk covers coding, debugging, browser-native AI, and upgrading websites for AI agents. Yohan demonstrates AI coding agents using skills—lightweight text-based plugins that add domain expertise and repeatable workflows, configured via agents.md. Olivier demonstrates the Chrome DevTools MCP server, exposing browser DevTools as agent-callable tools for navigation, screenshots, and performance testing across network speeds. Yohan then shows AI features built directly into Chrome DevTools: AI-powered error explanations, network request debugging, performance trace analysis, and live CSS modifications with apply-to-workspace capability. Olivier introduces Web AI APIs, a W3C draft standard enabling AI models to run locally in the browser. He demonstrates the Summarizer API for product review summarization and the Proofreader API for spelling correction with detailed correction output including start/end indices. Yohan demonstrates the Prompt API, a general-purpose multimodal API accepting text, images, and audio, using it to auto-generate product reviews from uploaded images with JSON schema constraints. Olivier notes these APIs are highly experimental, with Chrome flags required and API surfaces still changing. The session then covers upgrading websites for AI agents: LLMs.txt as a markdown file combining robots.txt and sitemap concepts to guide agents to documentation, and LLM-full.txt which bundles entire website content into a single file to give coding agents up-to-date framework references. Finally, Olivier demonstrates Web MCP, a highly experimental proposal for browser-embedded agentic browsing. He shows manually registering an add-to-cart tool on the navigator object with JSON schema and execute function, calling it from a Chrome extension and from an IDE agent. He then demonstrates a declarative approach: adding tool attributes to existing HTML forms to automatically transform them into MCP tools, with the browser generating schemas from form inputs, labels, and descriptions. A tool-auto-submit attribute enables agents to both fill and submit forms without human interaction. Olivier compares Web MCP readiness to responsive design adoption, urging developers to start experimenting now. Yohan and Olivier conclude that AI makes web developers' lives easier across coding, debugging, and performance, while developers must also prepare websites for AI agent consumption. LLMs.txt and MCP are already widespread; Web MCP is the next emerging standard.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.summary: Yohan and Olivier introduce themselves and outline the session covering AI across the web development lifecycle: coding, debugging, performance, browser-native AI APIs, and agentic web apps.

sections.title: AI Coding Agents and Skills
sections.summary: Yohan discusses skills as lightweight text-based plugins for coding agents, explaining their structure, contextual loading, and custom skill creation. He introduces the Seine demo app and shows an agent implementing a GitHub issue using skills for GitHub CLI, Playwright, local tunneling, and Telegram notifications, all configured via agents.md.

sections.title: Chrome DevTools MCP Demo
sections.summary: Olivier demonstrates the Chrome DevTools MCP server, which exposes browser DevTools as agent-callable tools. He shows an agent launching an app, navigating Chrome, taking screenshots, and running performance tests across three network speeds, producing reports with Core Web Vitals metrics and optimization suggestions.

sections.title: AI Features in Chrome DevTools
sections.summary: Yohan demonstrates AI-powered features built directly into Chrome DevTools: explaining CORS errors in the console with suggested fixes, debugging failing network requests via a built-in AI chat with application context, analyzing performance traces for LCP optimization hints, and live-editing CSS (adding a gradient to the Seine H1) with apply-to-workspace capability that writes changes back to source code.

sections.title: Web AI APIs and Summarizer Demo
sections.summary: Olivier introduces Web AI APIs as a W3C draft standard enabling AI models to run locally in the browser without internet calls or token costs. He demonstrates the Summarizer API on the Seine app, showing how to check browser support, create a summarizer with configurable type, length, input/output languages, and context, monitor the 4 GB model download, and generate a summary of product reviews.

sections.title: Proofreader and Prompt API Demos
sections.summary: Olivier demonstrates the Proofreader API for in-browser spelling correction, showing it correcting mistakes in a review input field and returning correction details with start/end indices. He also shows Chrome on-device internals for debugging model calls and token usage. Yohan then demonstrates the Prompt API, a general-purpose multimodal API accepting text, images, and audio, using it to auto-generate a product review from an uploaded image of damaged headphones with JSON schema constraints for structured output. Both APIs run entirely locally in the browser.

sections.title: Upgrading Websites for AI Agents: LLMs.txt and LLM-full.txt
sections.summary: Yohan introduces the need to optimize websites for AI agents alongside human usability and SEO. He presents LLMs.txt as a proposal combining robots.txt and sitemap concepts—a markdown file with links guiding AI agents to relevant documentation. He shows angular.dev's LLMs.txt as an example. He then introduces LLM-full.txt, which bundles entire website content including code examples into a single file, helping coding agents use the latest framework versions instead of relying on potentially outdated training data.

sections.title: Web MCP Introduction and Demo
sections.summary: Olivier introduces Web MCP as a proposal for browser-embedded agentic browsing, contrasting it with current agentic browsers that mimic human interactions via screenshots or DOM inspection. He demonstrates manually registering an add-to-cart tool on the navigator object with JSON schema and execute function, calling it from a Chrome extension and an IDE agent. He then shows a declarative approach: adding tool attributes to existing HTML forms to auto-generate MCP tools with schemas derived from form inputs, labels, and descriptions. A tool-auto-submit attribute enables agents to fill and submit forms without human interaction. Olivier compares Web MCP readiness to responsive design adoption, urging developers to experiment now. Yohan and Olivier conclude that AI improves web development across coding, debugging, and performance, while developers must prepare websites for AI agent consumption, with LLMs.txt and MCP already widespread and Web MCP emerging.

limitations: Agent-generated reports are not always produced unless explicitly requested
Agent behavior can vary between runs—sometimes generating screenshots or JSON reports unprompted, sometimes not
Skills are not always loaded into the agent context; they are pulled based on the description matching the current task
AI DevTools features are not enabled by default; users must manually enable them in DevTools settings under the AI innovation tab
Web AI APIs are still in W3C draft status and highly experimental; API surfaces can change, and not all browsers support them yet
Web AI APIs require enabling Chrome flags; browser support is limited (Chrome implementing, Edge coming, Opera partially implementing)
Coding agents' training data can be months or years out of date regarding framework content, necessitating LLM-full.txt for up-to-date references
Web MCP is very early-stage with minimal current documentation and APIs changing frequently
AI responses in DevTools can vary in verbosity between runs
Coding agents sometimes fail during demos (e.g., token not found, notification not received)
Web MCP demos experienced minor issues (form submission not visibly adding content on first attempt, file save delay)
Chrome is not yet an agentic IDE; Web MCP tool calling required a browser extension or external IDE agent during the demo

Summarizer API model download is approximately 4 GB
Summarizer API supports four types: TLDR, teaser, key points, headline
Prompt API supports input types: text, image, and audio (multimodal)
Web MCP add-to-cart tool called with five water bottles and three laptops
